examples.professional: Our two proposals are tied on cost, so we need a different criterion to decide.
examples.analytical: When two hypotheses are tied on the evidence, the choice depends on prior commitments.

nuance.analogy: Tied is like two runners crossing the finish line at the same instant.
nuance.etymology: From the verb tie, from Old English tīgan, to bind.
common_mistakes: Adding a second syllable and saying 'tie-ed.'
Using tied when you mean tied up; tied up refers to being busy or fastened.

senses.definition: The period of a live action roleplaying event when players are in character.
senses.example: During time in, our characters stayed in costume and argued about the stolen crown.

senses.definition: The point at which such a period begins.
senses.example: The organizers rang a bell to mark the start of time in, and everyone fell silent.

senses.definition: Used to announce the end of time out and the beginning of time in.
senses.example: Time in! Get back into your characters, everyone, the tavern scene starts now.

senses.definition: To record the start of one's day or shift at work.

core.definition: To record the start of your work shift, usually on a time clock or timekeeping app.

pronunciation.tip: As a phrasal verb, the stress falls on the particle in, not on time. Say the two words quickly, with the first word lighter and the second word clearly stressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a routine workplace action without positive or negative feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use time in mainly in workplaces that track hours with a time clock, badge or app, such as restaurants, hospitals and hourly jobs. In everyday speech, people more often say clock in, so time in sounds more like the language of software or company policy. You will often hear it with time out.

distinctions.note: Clock in is the everyday spoken verb in most American workplaces, while time in is more typical in written policies and timekeeping software.
Check in means arriving and reporting to a place, such as a hotel or airport, while time in means recording the start of work hours.

examples.everyday: Did you time in yet? The app won't let me start my shift.
examples.professional: Please make sure you time in through the scheduling app before your first break.
examples.analytical: Attendance data is only as reliable as the moment staff time in, which is why timekeeping systems record the exact start of each shift.

nuance.analogy: Like passing through a turnstile that records the moment you enter, time in marks the exact start of your work.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I time in my work' without a preposition or time; normally you time in at a specific time or on an app.
Using time in for arriving at a hotel or airport, where check in is correct.

senses.definition: US and Canada spelling of tire: The rubber covering on a wheel.
US spelling of tire: The metal rim of a wheel, especially that of a railroad locomotive.
senses.example: The locomotive's steel tire had worn thin after decades of hauling freight across the plains.

senses.definition: A child's apron covering the upper part of the body, and tied with tape or cord; a pinafore. Also tier.
senses.example: Grandma tied a clean tire over the toddler's dress before she started the messy pie.

senses.definition: A covering for the head; a headdress.
senses.example: The queen wore a golden tire studded with pearls at the coronation.

senses.definition: A tier, row, or rank.
senses.example: The stadium's top tire of seats offered the best view of the whole field.

senses.definition: To make sleepy or weary.
senses.example: Hours of hauling boxes in the heat will tire anyone, even the strongest movers.

senses.definition: To become sleepy or weary.
senses.example: After three hours of studying, I started to tire and reached for coffee.

senses.definition: To become bored or impatient (with).
senses.example: I tire of this book.

senses.definition: To bore.
senses.example: His endless jokes about golf started to tire everyone at the dinner table.

core.definition: The rubber covering around a car or bicycle wheel, filled with air so the vehicle can roll and grip the road.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final er is a reduced r-colored vowel, and it sounds the same as the start of 'tire' the verb. Don't confuse it with 'tired'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical, everyday word for a car part.
nuance.usage_note: Americans spell this word tire, and British English uses tyre. In the U.S. you say 'I have a flat tire' or 'The tires need air.' At a gas station or repair shop, tire is the normal word, and it is used in everyday conversation about cars and bicycles.

distinctions.note: Tyre is the British spelling, while tire is the standard American spelling for the same wheel covering.
A wheel is the whole rotating part, while the tire is only the rubber covering around the rim.

examples.everyday: I got a flat tire on the highway, so I called roadside assistance.
examples.professional: Our fleet manager ordered new tires for the delivery vans before winter.
examples.analytical: Tire pressure affects braking distance, which is why engineers treat the tire as part of the vehicle's safety system.

nuance.analogy: Like a rubber ring on a wheel, similar to the rubber on a bike wheel that grips the ground.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'tire', short for 'attire', meaning dress or equipment; the vehicle sense is a later development.
common_mistakes: Writing 'tyre' in American contexts, since that is the British spelling.
Confusing tire with tired; the car part and the feeling of sleepiness are different words.

tire.etymology: From Middle English *tiren*, *tirien*, *teorien*, from Old English *tȳrian*, *tēorian* (“to fail, cease, become weary, be tired, exhausted; tire, weary, exhaust”), of uncertain origin.

conversation.text: I need new tires before winter.
One of my tires looks low. Can you check the pressure?
Long drives tire me out more than a full day at work.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the Titans, a race of gods in Greek mythology.
senses.example: The ancient myths describe titanic beings who ruled the cosmos before the Olympian gods.

senses.definition: Having great size, or great force, power, or strength.
senses.example: The titanic waves crashed over the breakwater and flooded the harbor road.

senses.definition: Of a conflict or contest: involving equally powerful participants.
senses.example: The Senate race was a titanic struggle between two well-funded candidates.

senses.definition: Of or relating to titanium, especially tetravalent titanium.
senses.example: The titanic compounds in the sample were analyzed by spectroscopy.

senses.definition: Of a mineral, especially iron ore: containing titanium, or from which titanium may be extracted.
senses.example: Samples of the titanic magnetite from the Adirondacks showed high iron and titanium content.

core.definition: Very large, huge or powerful, used for enormous efforts, struggles or forces.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TAN. The first syllable is 'ty' and the last is a reduced 'ik'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, depending on context; it emphasizes great scale or effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use titanic in news, speeches and literary writing to describe huge struggles, battles or efforts, such as 'a titanic struggle.' It is not used for ordinary objects in casual conversation. The capitalized Titanic refers to the famous ship that sank in 1912.

distinctions.note: Huge is everyday and neutral for size, while titanic emphasizes epic scale or force, often in a contest.
Massive can describe weight or size in everyday speech, while titanic is more formal and dramatic.

examples.everyday: Moving that piano up the stairs was a titanic effort, and we're still sore.
examples.professional: Migrating the legacy system is a titanic task, so we need to split it into smaller phases.
examples.analytical: The essay traces the titanic struggle between state authority and religious conscience across the early modern period.

nuance.analogy: Like a mountain standing among hills, so much bigger than what surrounds it that it dominates the view.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Titanicus, from Titan, one of the Titans of Greek mythology.
common_mistakes: Using titanic for ordinary size, where huge or large is more natural.
Confusing the adjective titanic with the ship name, which is capitalized as Titanic.

senses.definition: Frankly, honestly.
senses.example: I don't mind, to be honest.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see to,‎ be,‎ honest.
senses.example: I tried to be honest but still no one believed me.

core.definition: A phrase used to introduce a frank opinion, admission or criticism that the speaker wants to state directly.

pronunciation.tip: The h in honest is silent, so start with a vowel. Stress 'AH' and reduce the final syllable to 'nust'. Do not pronounce it as 'HON-est'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals candor, but it can sound defensive if said often.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use to be honest in casual talk to share an opinion or admit something, often before a critique or a confession. It works well with friends, coworkers, and family, but overusing it can make listeners wonder what you usually say. A natural reply is 'I appreciate that' or 'Yeah, I figured.'

distinctions.note: Frankly is slightly more formal and suits serious opinions, while to be honest sounds more casual and conversational.
To tell you the truth is more personal and often introduces a confession, while to be honest can introduce either an opinion or a criticism.

collocations: to be honest, I don't know
to be honest, I'm not sure

examples.everyday: To be honest, I'd rather stay home tonight than go out in this rain.
examples.professional: To be honest, I think the timeline is too aggressive for the team we have.
examples.analytical: To be honest, the argument depends on a premise that the author never defends.

nuance.analogy: To be honest is like opening a window in a stuffy room: the speaker lets fresh air into the conversation.
nuance.etymology: Honest from Latin honestus, 'honorable, respected'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the h in honest, as in 'HON-est'.
Using to be honest too often, which can make the rest of your speech sound less candid.

conversation.text: To be honest, I'm not really into horror movies.
I didn't love the food, to be honest, but the service was great.
"Did you like the show?" "To be honest, I fell asleep halfway through."

senses.definition: Sycophantic; fawning.

core.definition: Behaving like a toady; excessively flattering and obedient to someone powerful or important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TOH, and say the middle 'dee' with a long e. The final 'ish' has a short i, like 'fish'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes servile flattery and implies a lack of dignity or integrity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'toadyish' mainly in journalism, political commentary, and literary criticism to describe people who flatter those in power. It is stronger than 'polite' and less formal than 'sycophantic', and it is almost always an insult. Calling a coworker toadyish directly would be harsh; saying it about a third party in private conversation is more typical.

distinctions.note: 'Sycophantic' is more formal and more common in serious writing; 'toadyish' is more colloquial and carries a sharper, more personal sting.
'Obsequious' stresses excessive eagerness to serve; 'toadyish' focuses on flattering someone in order to gain favor.
'Servile' describes complete submission and slavish obedience; 'toadyish' is narrower and focuses on flattery for advantage.

examples.everyday: I can't stand how toadyish he gets whenever the boss walks into the room.
examples.professional: The memo struck me as toadyish, praising leadership decisions that nobody on the team had actually reviewed.
examples.analytical: Machiavelli warns princes against flatterers whose praise conceals their own ambitions, a point that makes toadyish courtiers a recurring danger in political life.

nuance.analogy: Like a shadow that always leans toward the brightest light, bending itself to whoever holds the power.
nuance.etymology: From 'toady' (a servile flatterer) with the suffix '-ish'; 'toady' is of uncertain origin, possibly from 'toad-eater'.
common_mistakes: Using 'toadyish' to describe a neutral or friendly person; it always implies servility.
Confusing the adjective 'toadyish' with the noun 'toady'.
Stressing the second syllable or pronouncing 'toady' as 'toe-dee'.

senses.definition: Foolish behavior or speech.
Jewelry.
senses.example: She locked her grandmother's tomfoolery in the safe before the houseguests arrived.

core.definition: Silly, playful or foolish behavior that wastes time or annoys other people.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'fool', not on 'tom', and the last two syllables are reduced to 'uh-ree'. Many learners put the stress on the first syllable, so practice shifting it to the middle.

nuance.connotation: Negative to mildly disapproving. It suggests frivolous or distracting behavior, though it can be used humorously among friends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tomfoolery in a playful, slightly old-fashioned way, often as 'Cut out the tomfoolery' when a group is goofing around too much. It is less common in formal writing, where 'nonsense' or 'horseplay' is more typical. It is a good word to use with friends, coworkers or kids, but not with someone you are trying to impress.

distinctions.note: Horseplay is rough, physical play, while tomfoolery is foolish or silly behavior in general, including talk.
Shenanigans suggests mischief or sneaky trickery, often with a hint of dishonesty, while tomfoolery is more harmless and silly.
Nonsense refers to words or ideas that make no sense, whereas tomfoolery refers to silly actions or behavior.

examples.everyday: Stop the tomfoolery and help me carry these boxes before it gets dark.
examples.professional: The meeting turned into tomfoolery once the team started joking about the budget, so we had to restart the agenda.
examples.analytical: Much of the public tomfoolery surrounding celebrity politics distracts voters from the substantive questions they should be debating.

nuance.analogy: Tomfoolery is like a classroom that gets noisy with paper airplanes when the teacher steps out: silly, distracting and harmless, but it wastes time.
nuance.etymology: From tomfool (a fool), formed from the generic male name Tom and fool, plus the suffix -ery.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable ('TAHM-fool-ery') instead of 'fool'.
Using tomfoolery in serious, formal or emotional contexts, where it sounds dismissive.

senses.definition: Topical.
senses.example: The panel's discussion was very topic, covering the week's headlines and their effect on local voters.

senses.definition: A subject; a theme; a category or general area of interest.
senses.example: A society where a topic cannot be discussed, does not have free speech.

senses.definition: The entity or idea that a clause or sentence is about.
senses.example: In the sentence the bakery sells bread, the topic is the bakery, and the rest describes what it does.

senses.definition: A discussion thread.
senses.example: Please post your question in the forum topic about installation problems so others can help you.

senses.definition: A component similar to a message queue which supports multiple subscribers.
senses.example: The producer publishes sensor readings to a Kafka topic that several downstream services consume.

senses.definition: A musical sign intended to suggest a particular style or genre.
senses.example: The composer placed a hunting topic in the brass section to evoke the sound of a chase through the forest.

core.definition: The subject someone is talking, writing, or thinking about; the main theme of a conversation or text.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, so say TAH-pik and not tuh-PIK. The final syllable -ic is pronounced /ɪk/, not /aɪk/ as in 'like.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a subject without judging it, so it fits almost any conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use topic in everyday conversation, meetings, and writing, as in 'What's the topic?' or 'Can we change the topic?' For school subjects, Americans often say subject, and in essays they may say thesis or main idea. Topic sentence is a standard term in American writing classes.

distinctions.note: Subject is broader for school courses or a field of study, while topic is more specific to a conversation, article, or discussion.
Theme refers to an underlying message or idea in a work, while topic names what the work is about on the surface.
Issue suggests a problem or matter of public concern, while topic is a neutral word for any subject.

examples.everyday: Can we change the topic? I'm tired of talking about the construction on our street.
examples.professional: Let's put the hiring plan on the agenda as the first topic, so we have time to discuss it.
examples.analytical: The essay's central topic is the relationship between memory and identity, which it develops through three case studies.

nuance.analogy: A topic is like the label on a file folder, telling you what is inside before you open it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek topikos, meaning of places, from topos, place; via Latin topica, the title of Aristotle's work on argument.
common_mistakes: Saying discuss about the topic, when the correct form is discuss the topic.
Using topic for a school course, where subject is more natural.

topic.etymology: From Latin *topica*, from Ancient Greek *τοπικός* (“pertaining to a place, local, pertaining to a common place, or topic, topical”), from *τόπος* (“a place”).

senses.definition: An electric ray of the genus Torpedo.
senses.example: The marine biology class learned that the torpedo can deliver a shock strong enough to stun prey.

senses.definition: A similar projectile that can travel through space.
senses.example: The science fiction novel described a torpedo streaking across the void toward the alien mothership.

senses.definition: A naval mine.
senses.example: The destroyer swung wide to avoid a drifting torpedo that had broken free from its moorings.

senses.definition: Synonym of submarine sandwich.
senses.example: For lunch we ordered a big torpedo with salami, provolone, and extra peppers from the deli.

senses.definition: A professional gunman or assassin.
senses.example: The mob boss hired a torpedo from out of town to take care of the witness.

senses.definition: A small explosive device attached to the top of the rail to provide an audible warning when a train passes over it.
senses.example: The engineer slowed the train when the torpedo cracked loudly under the wheels, warning him of the work zone.

senses.definition: A kind of firework in the form of a small ball, or pellet, which explodes when thrown upon a hard object.
senses.example: The kids laughed as each torpedo popped and fizzed when they threw it onto the cracked sidewalk.

senses.definition: A focal ovoid swelling on the axons of Purkinje cells, observed in several diseases such as essential tremor and spinocerebellar ataxia.
senses.example: Pathologists noted a torpedo on the Purkinje axon in the tremor patient's cerebellum sample.

senses.definition: A woman's shoe with a pointed toe.
senses.example: She wore a black torpedo with a pointed toe to the office holiday party.

senses.definition: A large breast; a breast with a large nipple.
senses.example: The comedian's crude joke about her torpedo made the whole audience groan.

senses.definition: A marijuana cigarette.
senses.example: He rolled a torpedo at the campsite and passed it around the fire.

senses.definition: A thick marijuana cigarette.
senses.example: The thick torpedo he lit on the porch smelled sweet, and the neighbors noticed immediately.

senses.definition: A cigarette containing marijuana and crack cocaine.
senses.example: Police found a torpedo laced with crack cocaine tucked inside the car's glovebox.

senses.definition: A cylindrical explosive projectile that can travel quickly underwater and is used as a weapon.
senses.example: The submarine fired a torpedo at the enemy convoy, which sank within minutes.

senses.definition: (historical) An automobile with a streamlined profile and a folding or detachable soft top, and having the hood or bonnet line raised to be level with the car's waistline, resulting in a straight beltline from front to back.
senses.example: Collectors at the auction admired the 1930s torpedo roadster with its sleek, low-slung body.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To strike (a ship) with one or more torpedoes.
senses.example: The U-boat torpedoed the freighter just after dawn, leaving survivors adrift in the cold water.

senses.definition: To sink (a ship) with one or more torpedoes.
To undermine or destroy any endeavor with a powerful attack.

core.definition: A self-propelled underwater missile, fired from a ship, submarine, or aircraft, designed to hit and sink a ship.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PEE, the second syllable. Do not say tor-PEH-doh; the vowel in the middle is a long e, and the final vowel is a clear oh.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests destruction, sabotage, and violent attack, though the verb is also used for ruining plans.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use torpedo as a noun for the weapon, and as a verb for striking or sinking a ship. In everyday speech, the verb is extended to mean sabotaging a plan, deal, or proposal, as in 'the rival firm torpedoed our bid.' The electric ray sense is zoological and rare. Use the verb in figurative speech only when the damage is real and fairly sudden.

distinctions.note: A torpedo travels underwater, while a missile travels through air or space.
A mine waits passively in the water, while a torpedo is self-propelled and moves toward its target.

examples.everyday: Don't mention the cake, or you'll torpedo the surprise.
examples.professional: A rival vendor's leaked pricing torpedoed our bid for the county contract.
examples.analytical: A torpedo's effectiveness depends on its guidance, speed, and warhead, which together determine whether it hits its target.

nuance.analogy: Like a guided underwater missile that silently chases its target and strikes without warning.
nuance.etymology: From Latin torpedo, 'numbness' or 'electric ray,' from torpere, 'to be numb.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable wrongly as tor-PEH-doh.
Spelling the past tense as 'torpedod' instead of 'torpedoed.'

torpedo.etymology: * Borrowed from Latin *torpēdō* (“a torpedo fish; numbness, torpidity, electric ray”), from *torpeō* + *-ēdō*, from Proto-Indo-European **ster-* (“stiff”).

senses.definition: A twist of cloth or wreath, typically placed underneath and forming part of a crest (as an orle or wreath) and customarily shown with six twists, the first tincture being the tincture of the field, the second the tincture of the metal, and so on; rarely, it occurs as a charge.
senses.example: The herald painted the torse beneath the crest, six twists alternating silver and blue.

core.definition: In heraldry, a twisted roll of cloth or wreath placed on top of a helmet, forming the base of a crest.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single syllable that rhymes with 'force' without the f. Do not say 'TOR-see' or confuse it with 'torso', which means the trunk of the body.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Torse appears almost only in heraldry, in the description of coats of arms, in museum catalogs, and in genealogy or armorial writing. Most Americans will never use it, so you need it mainly for reading heraldic descriptions or talking about coats of arms with specialists.

distinctions.note: A wreath is a general circle of leaves or flowers. A torse is specifically the twisted cloth base of a crest, drawn in alternating tinctures.
Mantling is the decorative cloth hanging from the helmet, while the torse is the twisted band that sits between the helmet and the crest.

examples.everyday: The museum guide pointed out the torse on the family's crest, a twisted band in gold and blue.
examples.professional: The heraldic artist must draw the torse with six twists, alternating the tinctures of the field and the metal.
examples.analytical: The torse, by its customary six twists, marks the boundary between the helmet and the crest, and its alternating colors visually link the two.

nuance.analogy: A torse is like a twisted rope cushion placed under a sculpted figure, holding up the crest above the helmet.
nuance.etymology: From French torse, from Latin tortus, 'twisted', the past participle of torquere, 'to twist'.
common_mistakes: Confusing torse with torso, the body's trunk.
Assuming the torse is only a decorative wreath; in heraldry its twists and tinctures are defined by rule.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or achieved using torsion.

core.definition: Relating to torsion, the twisting of an object around its long axis by forces applied in opposite directions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, TOR. The '-sion' of the root torsion becomes 'shun', so the word has three syllables, with the last one reduced to 'nul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term from engineering and physics.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers, mechanics, physicists, and materials scientists use torsional all the time in American English. In everyday talk, Americans usually say 'twisting' or 'twist'. You would use torsional when describing a specific kind of load, vibration, or stiffness in a technical discussion.

distinctions.note: Rotational describes any turning motion. Torsional refers specifically to twisting strain or deformation within a body held fixed at one end.
Flexural refers to bending, while torsional refers to twisting. A beam can fail under either or both.

examples.everyday: The mechanic said the axle had some torsional wear, so he replaced it.
examples.professional: We need to run a torsional vibration analysis on the drive shaft before we approve the new motor.
examples.analytical: A torsional model treats the structure as resisting twist, and its predictions depend on the assumed boundary conditions.

nuance.analogy: Torsional force is like wringing out a wet towel: you hold one end, twist the other, and the material resists.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin torsionalis, related to torsion, from Latin tortio, 'a twisting', from torquere, 'to twist'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'TOR-see-ohn-al' with the -sion pronounced as 'see-ohn'; the ending is 'shun'.
Using torsional for any kind of turning; it means specifically twisting strain.

senses.definition: Clipping of tortoise.
senses.example: Our pet tort wandered slowly across the backyard after the spring rain.

senses.definition: Clipping of tortoiseshell (“a domestic cat, guinea pig, rabbit, or other animal whose fur has black, brown, and yellow markings; a tortie”).
senses.example: The shelter's tort kitten has black, orange, and cream markings on her fur.

senses.definition: A wrongful act, whether intentional or negligent, regarded as non-criminal and unrelated to a contract, which causes an injury and can be remedied in civil court, usually through the awarding of damages.
senses.example: The company faced a tort lawsuit after its faulty ladder injured a worker.

senses.definition: Synonym of tart (“sharp- or sour-tasting; (figuratively) keen, severe, sharp”)
senses.example: The grapefruit was so tort that even my sweetest friend winced at the first bite.

senses.definition: Synonym of taut (“stretched tight; under tension”).
senses.example: The climber kept the rope tort as she inched up the granite face.

senses.definition: Of a boat: watertight.
senses.example: The old sailboat was tort enough to survive the storm without taking on water.

core.definition: A civil wrong, other than breach of contract, that causes someone harm and can lead to a lawsuit for damages.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a clear American r. Do not add a vowel between the r and the t; it sounds like tort, not tor-ut.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a legal wrong that causes injury, such as negligence in a car accident.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tort in legal, business, and insurance contexts. Lawyers and business people say 'a personal injury tort' or 'tort reform.' In casual speech, people say they are suing someone or that something was negligent. Do not confuse it with a crime, which is a wrong against the public.

distinctions.note: A crime is prosecuted by the government and can bring jail time. A tort is a civil wrong that the injured party sues over for money.
A breach of contract is a failure to meet a promise in an agreement. A tort is a wrong that exists regardless of any contract.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's dog bit me, and my lawyer says that's a tort, so I might sue for damages.
examples.professional: Our legal team flagged the claim as a tort, so it will go to the insurance carrier before the contract issue is addressed.
examples.analytical: Tort law expresses a moral intuition that those who injure others owe a remedy, even when no promise was broken.

nuance.analogy: A tort is like a broken window in someone else's house: you owe the owner for the damage, even without a signed agreement.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French tort, 'wrong,' from Latin tortum, 'twisted, wrong,' from torquere, 'to twist.'
common_mistakes: Confusing tort with crime; a tort is a civil wrong, while a crime is prosecuted by the state.
Pronouncing it with an extra vowel, as in tor-ut.

tort.etymology: From Middle English *tort* (“ wrong; an injury, a wrong”), from Old French *tort* (“misdeed, wrong”), from Medieval Latin *tortum* (“injustice, wrong”), a noun use of a neuter singular participle form of Latin *tortus* (“crooked; twisted”), the perfect…

senses.definition: The state of being total.
An aggregate quantity obtained by addition.
senses.example: the totality of your offspring

senses.definition: The phase of an eclipse when it is total.
senses.example: Clouds covered the sky, but the totality lasted nearly four minutes over our town.

core.definition: The whole of something considered as one complete thing; the entire amount or collection of it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TAL. The final -ity is a reduced ih followed by a clear tee sound, not two long vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes completeness without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use totality in formal writing and speech, as in the totality of the evidence or in its totality. In everyday talk, people say the whole thing, everything or the whole picture. Totality is also the everyday term for the phase of a total solar eclipse, as in the path of totality across the United States in 2017 and 2024.

distinctions.note: Whole is everyday; totality stresses the complete collection considered together.
Entirety stresses the state of being complete; totality stresses the sum of all the parts.
Total is the number you get from adding; totality is the complete set of things, not a sum.

examples.everyday: We drove four hours to get into the path of totality for the solar eclipse.
examples.professional: I would like to review the totality of the customer complaints before we change the policy.
examples.analytical: Theology often claims that God governs the totality of creation, not merely its spiritual or human parts.

nuance.analogy: Like looking at the whole pizza instead of just one slice.
nuance.etymology: From total (Late Latin totalis) plus the suffix -ity (Latin -itas).
common_mistakes: Using totality for a simple receipt total; say total there.
Using it in casual talk to mean everything, which sounds stiff.

senses.definition: The process of towing away a vehicle.

core.definition: The removal of an illegally parked or abandoned vehicle by a tow truck, usually at the owner's expense.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'TOH', with a lighter secondary stress on 'way'. The middle vowel is a weak schwa, so say 'TOH-uh-way', not 'toe-AWAY'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a costly, frustrating event for the vehicle owner.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'towaway' mostly in official notices, parking signs ('tow-away zone'), police reports and insurance language. In conversation, people usually say 'my car got towed'. As a noun, it works in sentences like 'The towaway cost me three hundred dollars.' A natural reply is 'Ugh, that's rough. Where did they take it?'

distinctions.note: An impound is the holding of a vehicle in a lot, while a towaway is the removal itself; the car may be impounded after a towaway.
'Tow' is the general act of pulling a vehicle, while a towaway is the specific removal of an illegally parked or abandoned car.

examples.everyday: I got a towaway from outside the grocery store, so I am headed downtown to get my car.
examples.professional: Dispatch logged twelve towaways on Fifth Street before the street-cleaning shift began.
examples.analytical: Towaway policies raise fairness questions when the fines fall hardest on drivers who can least afford them.

nuance.analogy: A towaway is the parking version of a sudden eviction: the car is gone before the owner can object.
nuance.etymology: From the phrasal verb tow away, meaning to tow a vehicle off.
common_mistakes: Using 'towaway' as a verb; the verb is 'tow away'.
Mixing spellings: 'towaway' is the noun, while signs often read 'tow-away zone' as an adjective.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'toh-uh-WAY'.

senses.definition: In AI: Tensor processing unit: a chip designed specifically for machine learning workloads.
Initialism of thermoplastic polyurethane, a type of plastic; its applications include 3D printing.
senses.example: The phone case is made of TPU, which stays flexible even in cold weather.

senses.definition: Initialism of Tensor Processing Unit, a circuit optimized for neural network machine learning.

core.definition: Tensor Processing Unit: a specialized chip, designed by Google, that speeds up machine learning computations, especially neural network training.

pronunciation.tip: Say the three letters separately, as tee-pee-you, with the main stress on the last syllable. Don't say it as one word, and don't confuse it with the plastic also abbreviated TPU.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term with no emotional charge, though teams sometimes debate its cost against GPUs.
nuance.usage_note: In AI work, Americans say TPU for Google's custom accelerator, usually in cloud settings such as 'Cloud TPU'. In a manufacturing or 3D-printing context, the same letters mean thermoplastic polyurethane, so always check the domain. In meetings, people often ask whether a model can run on TPUs or GPUs.

distinctions.note: A GPU is a general-purpose parallel processor used for graphics and many computing tasks, while a TPU is built specifically for the matrix operations used in machine learning.
A CPU handles general-purpose computing with a few powerful cores, whereas a TPU is an accelerator that handles large numerical workloads much faster for neural networks.

examples.everyday: My friend's team trains their image models on TPUs in Google Cloud because it's faster than their old setup.
examples.professional: Before we move the training job to TPUs, we need to confirm that our framework supports them.
examples.analytical: The cost trade-off between TPUs and GPUs depends on how well a workload fits the chip's matrix-multiplication units.

nuance.analogy: A TPU is like a specialized kitchen appliance built for one recipe: it does that job far better than a general-purpose kitchen, but it isn't useful for everything.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of 'tensor processing unit'; 'tensor' comes from Latin tendere, 'to stretch'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the AI meaning with thermoplastic polyurethane in a manufacturing context.
Saying it as one word, 'tee-pu', instead of three letters.

conversation.text: A TPU is a custom chip designed specifically for the tensor operations used in neural networks.
Porting the training code to TPUs required changes to how we handled data loading.
TPUs are mainly available through one cloud provider, so choosing them is also a vendor decision.

senses.definition: A long walk.
senses.example: I would drive to the shops from here; you can walk, but it's quite a trek.

senses.definition: A slow or difficult journey.
senses.example: We're planning a trek up Kilimanjaro.

senses.definition: To journey on foot, especially to hike through mountainous areas.
senses.example: On our summer break we decided to trek through the mountains of northern Montana for a week.

senses.definition: To make a slow or arduous journey.
senses.example: After the blizzard, the road crew had to trek through deep snow to reach the stranded cars.

core.definition: A long, difficult walk or journey, often on foot through rough or mountainous country.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short e, rhyming with 'neck' and 'check'. The r is strong and the k is clearly released.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting adventure and effort; it can be used humorously for any tiring trip.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trek for a long hike, a trip to a faraway place, or even a tiring errand, such as 'the trek to the DMV'. It is informal and friendly. Used as a verb, it often means to hike on foot through difficult terrain.

distinctions.note: A hike is usually a walk on trails for recreation, while a trek is longer, harder, and often implies a journey with a destination.
Journey is neutral and general, while trek emphasizes effort, distance, or difficulty.

examples.everyday: That was a long trek to the grocery store in this heat, but the mangoes were worth it.
examples.professional: The data team had a long trek from the old server room to the new cloud migration plan, but we finally finished it.
examples.analytical: Her intellectual trek from empiricism to theology traces a path that many thinkers have walked before her.

nuance.analogy: A trek is like a marathon of the feet: it is longer and harder than a stroll.
nuance.etymology: From Afrikaans 'trek', a journey or migration, from Dutch 'trekken', to pull or draw.
common_mistakes: Using trek for a short or easy walk.
Pronouncing it with a long e like 'treek'.

trek.etymology: From *trek*, from Dutch *trekken*, from Middle Dutch *trekken* and *treken* (“to trek, place, bring, move”), from **trekkan*, **trekan*, from **trekan*, from Proto-Germanic **trekaną*, **trakjaną* (“to drag, haul, scrape, pull”), from Proto-Indo-European…

conversation.text: It's a bit of a trek to the beach from here, like twenty minutes.
We had to trek all the way back to the car in the rain.
They're planning a ten-day trek in the mountains.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being tremendous.

core.definition: The quality of being tremendous, meaning very great in size, force, or extent, or sometimes wonderfully impressive.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MEN, and the final -ous and -ness syllables are weak schwas. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce the middle vowel as a clear 'ay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes size or force, and can be positive when it means impressiveness. Context decides whether it sounds awe-struck or threatening.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use the noun tremendousness in conversation. They say 'how tremendous' or 'the size of it' instead. You will mostly meet it in essays, reviews, or formal writing about scale or power. For everyday talk, use huge, enormous, or amazing.

distinctions.note: Magnitude is a measurable quantity, often technical. Tremendousness is a more impressionistic sense of how overwhelming something is.
Enormity suggests something monstrous or morally shocking, while tremendousness is neutral or admiring about great size or force.

examples.professional: The tremendousness of the migration scope surprised everyone, so we split it into three phases.
examples.analytical: Otto's account of the holy depends on a felt sense of the tremendousness of the sacred, which exceeds rational comprehension.

nuance.analogy: Like the sky at night, its tremendousness is felt before it is measured.
nuance.etymology: From tremendous, from Latin tremendus, 'to be trembled at', from tremere 'to tremble'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as TREM-en-dous; the main stress is on MEN.
Using tremendousness for everyday praise; say 'It was tremendous' or 'It was amazing' instead.

senses.definition: One who trespasses; an interloper.
senses.example: The sign warned that any trespasser would be prosecuted, but the teenagers climbed the fence anyway.

core.definition: A person who enters someone else's land or property without permission, or who violates another person's rights.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable; the middle syllable is weak and says 'puss' in a reduced way. Do not stress the second syllable, as in 'tres-PASS-er'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying someone who has entered where they do not belong; the tone is more neutral in legal or warning contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trespasser most often on signs, in news reports and in legal discussions, such as 'Trespassers will be prosecuted.' In everyday talk people often say 'someone who came onto my property' instead. The term can also appear in religious or literary writing to mean a person who has wronged another.

distinctions.note: An intruder forces their way in, often suddenly or violently; a trespasser may simply walk onto land without permission.
A burglar enters to steal, which is a separate crime; a trespasser is defined by entering without permission, whatever the purpose.
A visitor is invited; a trespasser is not, so the difference lies entirely in permission.

examples.everyday: The neighbor's dog chased a trespasser out of our backyard last night.
examples.professional: Our security team logs every trespasser who enters the restricted lab area after hours.
examples.analytical: The parable turns the trespasser into a figure of unexpected mercy, forcing the listener to reconsider who truly belongs.

nuance.analogy: A trespasser is like a guest who walks into your living room without knocking and never gets invited.
nuance.etymology: From trespass (verb), from Old French trespasser, to pass across or beyond, plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'tres-PASS-er', instead of TRES-pus-er.
Saying trespasser on the property instead of trespasser on the property is acceptable, but do not say trespasser into the field, which sounds unnatural.

senses.definition: Having no pleasing tune; not tuneful.
senses.example: The tuneless humming from the next room drove me crazy during the entire afternoon.

senses.definition: Silent or mute.
senses.example: After the accident, the singer stood tuneless on stage, unable to utter a single note.

core.definition: Lacking a pleasant melody, or sung or played without musical accuracy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending '-less' is reduced to 'lus', not a long e sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes a sound or performance as unpleasant or off-key, though people often say it humorously.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tuneless to describe singing or whistling that sounds off-key or unpleasant. Calling someone's singing tuneless can be unkind, so say it lightly among friends. A more polite option is 'not a great singer' or 'a little off-key'.

distinctions.note: Off-key is the everyday idiom for singing the wrong pitch, while tuneless describes an overall lack of melody.
Monotonous means dull and unvarying in pitch or tone, while tuneless means lacking a pleasing tune at all.
Tone-deaf describes a person who cannot tell pitches apart, while tuneless describes the sound that results.

examples.everyday: He hummed tunelessly while he washed the dishes, and everyone in the kitchen smiled.
examples.professional: The voice actor's read is tuneless, so the emotional beats in the script get lost.
examples.analytical: A tuneless chant can still carry meaning, but liturgy often relies on melody to make words memorable.

nuance.analogy: A tuneless song is like a sentence with the wrong rhythm: the words are all there, but the shape is missing.
nuance.etymology: From tune plus the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Using tuneless to describe the quality of a speaking voice; it refers to melody and pitch in music.

senses.definition: (dated) To avert; to stop (something).
senses.example: Let us pray that God will turn off this plague from our city.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To leave a road; to exit a highway or other main road.
senses.example: You'll need to turn off before we get to the county line.

senses.definition: To rotate a tap or valve so as to interrupt the outflow of liquid or gas.
senses.example: Remember to turn the tap off once you've finished so you don't waste water.

senses.definition: To power down, to switch off, to put out of operation, to deactivate (an appliance, light, mechanism, functionality etc.).
senses.example: Turn off the machine and unplug it when you leave.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see turn,‎ off.
senses.example: He turned off from me and faced the far wall.

senses.definition: To deactivate a heat source cooking a particular item.
senses.example: You can turn off the green beans now.

senses.definition: To become deactivated; to become powered down.
senses.example: My computer turned off!

senses.definition: To bore, repulse, disgust, or discourage (someone).
senses.example: That book's plot was so predictable, it turned me off.

senses.definition: To raise, unblocking the way and signaling that a train may proceed.
senses.example: The signalman turned off the semaphore arm so the freight train could proceed.

core.definition: To stop a device or light from working by switching it off, or to make someone lose interest or dislike something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress OFF strongly. In the cot-caught merger, off may sound like 'awf' or 'ahf' depending on region, and both are acceptable; make the final f clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for devices; negative when describing a person, as in 'that turns me off.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it constantly for appliances, lights, and water: 'Turn off the stove before you leave.' Figuratively, 'that turns me off' means something bores or repels you, which can sound harsh if said about a person. Turn off your phone is common at meetings and movies.
word_family: turn-off (noun): something that bores or repels someone

distinctions.note: Shut off is a near-synonym often used for water or power supply; turn off is the most common everyday word.
Switch off is common for electrical devices and suggests a switch; turn off is broader.
Turn off stops something completely; turn down only lowers it.

collocations: turn off at the next exit

examples.everyday: Did you turn off the stove before we left the house?
examples.professional: Please turn off your camera during the screen share so the call runs smoothly.
examples.analytical: Some readers turn off a philosopher after the first chapter, yet the argument rewards patience.

nuance.analogy: Like closing a faucet until nothing flows out.
nuance.etymology: Turn from Old English turnian; off from Old English of.
common_mistakes: Putting the wrong word order: 'turn it off' and 'turn off the light' are both correct, but 'turn off it' is not.
Confusing turn off with turn down: a dimmer is turned down, not off.

conversation.text: Turn off the lights when you leave.
Please turn your phones off during the movie.
The rude waiter really turned me off that restaurant.
Rude service really turns me off.
Turn off at the next exit.
Turn off the engine while you pump gas.
Don't forget to turn off the stove.
Turn off the water while you brush your teeth.

related: turn-off (noun): something that bores or repels someone

senses.definition: To flip over; to rotate uppermost to bottom.
senses.example: Turn over the box and look at the bottom.

senses.definition: To relinquish; give back.
senses.example: They turned over the evidence to the authorities.

senses.definition: To transfer.
senses.example: She agreed to turn over the company's accounts to the new auditor before Friday.

senses.definition: To produce, complete, or cycle through.
senses.example: They can turn over about three hundred units per hour.

senses.definition: To generate (a certain amount of money from sales).
senses.example: The business turned over several million last year.

senses.definition: To mull, ponder.
senses.example: He turned over the job offer in his mind all night before deciding.

senses.definition: To spin the crankshaft of an internal combustion engine using the starter or hand crank in an attempt to make it run.
senses.example: My old pickup wouldn't start, so I had to turn over the engine several times.

senses.definition: To cause extensive disturbance or disruption to (a room, storage place, etc.), e.g. while searching for an item, or ransacking a property.
senses.example: I've turned over the whole place, but I still can't find my glasses.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see turn,‎ over.
To give up control (of the ball and thus the ability to score).
senses.example: The Giants didn't turn the ball over in their last four games.

core.definition: To flip something so its other side faces up, or to hand something over to someone else.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on oh in over, and the final -er is a weak American r-colored vowel, so it sounds like 'OH-ver', not 'oh-VER'. Keep the t in turn clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a physical flip or a formal transfer of responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use turn over for flipping food or a page and for handing over responsibility or documents: 'Turn the report over to the manager.' In business it sounds professional and clear. In a car context, 'the engine won't turn over' means it will not start. Remember that you turn something over, and you turn it over to a person.

distinctions.note: Hand over is neutral and general; turn over often implies formally transferring responsibility, documents or property.
Flip is informal and quick; turn over is neutral and can describe slower or more deliberate movement.
Overturn means to reverse a decision or to tip something over; turn over is about movement or transfer.

collocations: turn over the evidence to the police

examples.everyday: Turn the pancake over when the edges start to look dry.
examples.professional: Please turn the final report over to the client by Friday so they can review it.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the archive was turned over to the state without any real review.

nuance.analogy: Like flipping a card face-down to show the other side.
nuance.etymology: Turn from Old English tyrnan; over from Old English ofer.
common_mistakes: Placing the object wrongly: say 'turn it over', not 'turn over it'.
Confusing turn over (transfer) with hand in (submit), which is used in school and work.

senses.definition: Furnished with tusks; having tusks.

core.definition: Having tusks, the long, pointed teeth that project from the mouth of animals such as elephants, walruses and wild boars.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first and only main syllable. The -ed ending is pronounced as a plain /t/ after the k sound, so the word is one syllable, not 'TUSK-ed'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a plain descriptive word with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: You will mostly meet 'tusked' in nature writing, zoology, wildlife documentaries and descriptions of animals. In everyday talk Americans usually say 'an elephant with tusks' or 'a long-tusked boar', because 'with tusks' sounds more natural in speech.

distinctions.note: 'Toothed' means having teeth in general, while 'tusked' refers specifically to long, projecting teeth like tusks.
'With tusks' is the more natural spoken form; 'tusked' is shorter and more descriptive, typical of writing.

examples.everyday: We saw a big tusked elephant standing by the water hole on our safari.
examples.professional: The wildlife report notes that the tusked males in this herd are the main targets of poachers.
examples.analytical: The painter's tusked boar becomes a symbol of untamed nature, its weapons marking the line between wilderness and the domestic farm.

nuance.analogy: A tusk is like an overgrown front tooth that kept growing outward, and 'tusked' simply describes an animal that has them.
nuance.etymology: From 'tusk' (from Old English tusc) plus the adjective suffix -ed.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable and saying 'TUSK-id' instead of one syllable 'tuskt'.
Using 'tusked' for any animal with big teeth, when it means specifically tusks.

senses.definition: Nietzsche's "overman" or "superman": a person who creates their own values instead of accepting inherited morality.
senses.example: Nietzsche's ideal ubermensch creates his own values rather than obeying inherited morality.

core.definition: In Nietzsche's philosophy, a person who creates their own values rather than accepting inherited moral rules.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, YOO, with a secondary stress on MENSH. The German 'ü' becomes an English 'oo' sound, and the final 'sh' is a clear American sh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy, but it can be negative in popular use because it has been linked with arrogance and with misreadings of Nietzsche.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ubermensch almost only in philosophy classes, literary discussion, or writing about Nietzsche. In casual talk, people would more likely say superman, although that refers to the comic character. Because the term has been misused for elitism, using it in an argument may invite challenge, so explain your meaning.

distinctions.note: Superman is a comic book hero, while the ubermensch is a philosophical ideal of self-created values in Nietzsche's writing.

collocations: the will to power and the ubermensch

examples.everyday: My roommate is reading Nietzsche, and he keeps talking about the ubermensch.
examples.professional: In the ethics workshop, we discussed how the ubermensch concept shapes modern debates about self-improvement.
examples.analytical: Nietzsche's ubermensch is not a biological type but a figure who overcomes inherited morality through creative self-legislation.

nuance.analogy: The ubermensch is like a sculptor who carves his own statue from raw stone rather than copying the statues he was handed.
nuance.etymology: From German über, meaning over or beyond, and Mensch, meaning human; coined by Friedrich Nietzsche.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (yoo-ber-MENSH); the primary stress falls on the first syllable.
Treating ubermensch as a fictional superhero term; in philosophy it refers to Nietzsche's idea.

senses.definition: Extremely conservative, especially in politics.
senses.example: The John Birch Society is an ultraconservative political group in the USA.

senses.definition: A person or group with extremely conservative views.
senses.example: The ultraconservative senator refused to support any bill that expanded federal spending.

core.definition: Holding extremely conservative views, especially in politics or religion, and far more traditional or resistant to change than most conservatives.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable is 'ul', not 'ool' or 'uh'. Stress falls on 'SUR' in conservative, and the rest of the word is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Often negative or politically charged, depending on the speaker. Opponents use it as criticism, while supporters may prefer traditionalist or conservative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ultraconservative in news and political discussion to describe very far-right positions, such as strict opposition to most reforms. Because it is a loaded label, people on the other side may take it as an insult. In casual talk, many Americans would say very conservative or far right instead.

distinctions.note: Conservative describes moderate or mainstream traditional views. Ultraconservative means the views are at the extreme end of that range.
Far-right is a broader political-spectrum term that can include extremist groups. Ultraconservative focuses on the degree of conservatism in views.

examples.everyday: My uncle has become pretty ultraconservative lately, and we usually avoid talking about politics at dinner.
examples.professional: The team said the new policy would alienate ultraconservative customers, so marketing should avoid that message.
examples.analytical: Scholars distinguish ultraconservative movements, which seek to restore an earlier order, from ordinary conservatives who accept gradual change.

nuance.analogy: An ultraconservative view is like a thermostat turned all the way toward the past, leaving no room for new settings.
nuance.etymology: From ultra- 'beyond' plus conservative, from Latin conservare 'to preserve'.
common_mistakes: Writing it as ultra-conservative with a hyphen; both forms are used, but the closed form is common.
Using it as a neutral description without realizing many listeners will hear it as criticism.

senses.definition: To unfasten.
senses.example: Please unbuckle your seatbelt and stay seated until the plane comes to a full stop.

core.definition: To undo the buckle or fastening of a belt, strap, seatbelt or shoe.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BUK, the second syllable, and the vowel is a short uh sound, not 'oo'. The -le ending is a syllabic l, so the word ends in 'kuhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, practical verb used in everyday safety and daily-life situations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unbuckle constantly with seatbelts, car seats, backpacks, belts and straps. A natural reply to a request is 'Okay, I'm unbuckling now.' Americans say 'unbuckle your seatbelt' in cars and on planes, and the word stays neutral and polite in all these settings.

distinctions.note: Unfasten is a general word for undoing any fastening; unbuckle is specific to buckles, belts and straps.
Unzip is for zippers; unbuckle is for buckles, so do not use unzip for a seatbelt.

examples.everyday: Hold on, let me unbuckle my seatbelt so I can grab my bag.
examples.professional: Before the field test, unbuckle the equipment harness and check the sensor mounts for wear.
examples.analytical: The safety argument turns on whether passengers can unbuckle their restraints quickly in an emergency without help.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling the metal tongue out of a belt's hole, so the strap falls loose.
nuance.etymology: From un- and buckle; buckle comes from Old French boucle, from Latin buccula, cheek strap.
common_mistakes: Using unbuckle for zippers, locks or doors, which need different verbs.
Stressing the first syllable un- instead of BUK.

senses.definition: Not characteristic.
senses.example: Her quiet decision to shout at the referee was uncharacteristic of such a patient coach.

senses.definition: Out of character; behavior that is unusual for a given person or thing.

core.definition: Not typical of a particular person or thing; unlike the way someone usually behaves or the way something usually is.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on RIS, the third syllable of 'characteristic', not on the first syllable of 'character'. The middle vowels are weak, so the word moves quickly from KAIR to RIS.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a break from someone's normal behavior, which can be positive, negative, or simply surprising depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in everyday talk and in news or workplace comments, as in 'That's uncharacteristic of him.' It is slightly formal compared with 'out of character,' which is the more casual phrase. It is often followed by 'of' and a person's name or pronoun.

distinctions.note: Atypical is more statistical and neutral, describing something unlike the usual type; uncharacteristic focuses on a person's known pattern.
Unusual is general and describes anything rare; uncharacteristic compares behavior with a known personal or group pattern.
Out of character is the casual phrase used in conversation; uncharacteristic is more precise and suits written or formal speech.

examples.everyday: Dan skipped our Friday lunch, which is uncharacteristic of him, so I texted to make sure he was okay.
examples.professional: The spike in error rates was uncharacteristic for this service, so I checked the upstream data before blaming the model.
examples.analytical: The author's uncharacteristic restraint in this chapter suggests a deliberate break from the polemical tone of her earlier work.

nuance.analogy: Like a usually quiet dog suddenly barking at everyone: the change stands out because it breaks a clear pattern.
nuance.etymology: Un- 'not' plus characteristic, from Greek kharaktēristikos 'marking, distinctive', from kharaktēr 'engraved mark'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable of characteristic; the strong stress is on RIS.
Using uncharacteristic about a thing with no known pattern; it works best when there is an established norm to break.

senses.definition: Not computable; that cannot be computed.

core.definition: Impossible to calculate or determine by any algorithm or mechanical procedure, no matter how much time is available.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PYOO, the third syllable, and the final -able is a weak bul sound. Do not add an extra syllable after the p, and remember that compute drops its final e before -able, so the spelling is computable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical description rather than a judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in mathematics, computer science and philosophy of mind. In everyday talk they say cannot be calculated or impossible to work out. In technical writing it has a precise meaning: no algorithm can produce the answer, as with the halting problem. Outside that context it can sound inflated.

distinctions.note: Intractable describes a problem that is computable in principle but too hard to solve in practice; uncomputable means no algorithm can solve it at all.
Undecidable describes a yes-or-no question that no algorithm can settle; uncomputable more broadly describes a function or number that no algorithm can produce.
Incomputable is an older, less common variant; uncomputable is the standard term in most American technical writing.

examples.everyday: I tried to work out the split for the group dinner, but the bill was so messy it felt uncomputable.
examples.professional: Whether the Kolmogorov complexity of a string is uncomputable matters for how we design our compression benchmarks.
examples.analytical: Turing showed that the halting problem is uncomputable, which limits what any program can prove about other programs.

nuance.analogy: Like a question that no finite set of instructions can answer for every possible case.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus computable, from Latin computare 'to reckon together'.
common_mistakes: Using it for hard but solvable problems; intractable is the better word for those.
Writing computeable with an extra e; the correct spelling is computable.

senses.definition: Insufficiently parameterized.

core.definition: Having too few parameters to capture the patterns in the data, so a model fits the training data poorly.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on RAM, and the word ends in a clear -ized sound. Don't reduce the middle syllables so much that the word sounds like 'un-der-PAR-ma-rized'; keep the schwa in puh and the r in -der and -ter.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a technical description of a model; it is a flaw, but not an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists use this word in model-selection discussions, papers and code reviews. Americans usually say 'the model is underparameterized' rather than 'has underparameterization.' Its opposite is overparameterized, and both appear often in deep learning discussions.

distinctions.note: An underparameterized model is too simple to learn the signal, so it underfits; an overfit model learns noise from too much flexibility.
Underfit describes the result (poor fit to training data); underparameterized describes the cause (too few parameters).

examples.everyday: My phone's voice assistant keeps mishearing me, so I guess its model is a bit underparameterized for my accent.
examples.professional: The first baseline looks underparameterized, so let's add interaction terms before we blame the training data.
examples.analytical: A model is underparameterized when its hypothesis class cannot represent the target function, which forces systematic bias regardless of sample size.

nuance.analogy: Like trying to draw a detailed portrait with only three crayons: you simply do not have enough tools to capture the detail.
nuance.etymology: Formed from under- plus parameterized, from parameter (from Greek para-, beside, and metron, measure).
common_mistakes: Saying 'underparametrized' with one e; Americans in technical writing usually write 'parameterized'.
Using it to mean 'poorly trained' rather than having too few parameters.

senses.definition: Not deserved, earned or merited; unjustifiable or unfair.

core.definition: Not earned or merited; received without deserving it, often in a way that seems unfair.

pronunciation.tip: Secondary stress is on UN and primary stress on ZERVD, the second half of the word. The final -ed is silent after v, so say 'zurvd' with no extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Often negative or emotional, as it suggests injustice; it can also be neutral when describing a lucky break.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use undeserved in conversation and writing to describe praise, blame, luck or punishment that seems unfair. You might say 'undeserved criticism' in an office or 'undeserved luck' with friends. A natural reply to a compliment you do not accept is 'I don't know if I deserve that.'

distinctions.note: Unearned often refers to money or privilege without work; undeserved emphasizes that a person does not merit the outcome, good or bad.
Unjust describes a whole system or act as wrong; undeserved describes a specific outcome that the person did not merit.

examples.everyday: My coworker got all the credit for my project, which felt undeserved.
examples.professional: The manager's public criticism of the team was undeserved, since the delay came from vendor data.
examples.analytical: Grace, in the theological tradition, is by definition a gift given to those who have not earned it, so it is undeserved.

nuance.analogy: Like a parking ticket for a car that was legally parked, an undeserved outcome is a penalty or reward that does not match what you did.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus deserve, from Latin deservire, to serve zealously.
common_mistakes: Confusing undeserved with 'undesirable', which means unwanted.
Saying 'undeserved' for something that was simply unpaid; use 'unpaid' or 'unearned' for money.

senses.definition: In a way, or to an extent, that is not disputed.
senses.example: He is undisputedly the best pitcher the franchise has ever had.

core.definition: In a way that no one disagrees with or challenges; beyond any reasonable argument.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'pute', the middle of 'dispute', and the 'pyoo' sound is a long u. The final '-edly' reduces to 'id-lee', and the 't' between vowels can be a flap in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It is used to emphasize strong agreement, often for praise or superiority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say 'undisputed' as an adjective or 'indisputably' as an adverb. 'Undisputedly' is understood and acceptable, but it sounds more literary than everyday. In conversation, Americans might say 'no question, he's the best' instead.

distinctions.note: Indisputably is the more common American adverb and carries a stronger sense that no argument is possible, while undisputedly stresses that no one is currently challenging the claim.
Unquestionably focuses on certainty of truth, while undisputedly focuses on general acceptance by others.

examples.everyday: He's undisputedly the best pizza maker on our street, and nobody on the block would argue with that.
examples.professional: The Postgres cluster is undisputedly our most reliable datastore, so we should build the new service on top of it.
examples.analytical: Newton's laws were undisputedly accepted for two centuries before relativity forced a revision of their domain.

nuance.analogy: Like a verdict that everyone in the room has accepted, so no one raises an objection.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus disputed, from Latin disputare 'to discuss, argue', from dis- plus putare 'to think, reckon'.
common_mistakes: Using 'undisputedly' where 'indisputably' sounds more natural to American ears.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in un-dis-PYOOT-id-lee, rather than the first stress on 'pute'.

senses.definition: Not eatable; not fit for eating.
senses.example: The casserole left in the fridge for a month had become completely uneatable.

core.definition: So unpleasant, spoiled, or badly made that it is not fit to eat.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EE, the second syllable. Between vowels the t is often a quick flap that sounds like a soft d, so it is closer to un-EE-duh-buhl in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes food, usually in casual complaint, and can sound harsh if said about someone's cooking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use uneatable to complain about bad food, as in the burnt toast was uneatable. It is informal and mostly about taste or condition. For food that is harmful or not food at all, say inedible instead, and saying uneatable about a host's cooking can be rude.

distinctions.note: Inedible means not safe or not meant to be eaten, while uneatable usually means it is edible but tastes terrible or is spoiled.
Unpalatable describes something unpleasant to taste or hard to accept, and it can be used figuratively for ideas or facts.
Disgusting is a strong emotional reaction to something repulsive, while uneatable is a practical judgment about food.

examples.everyday: The fish at that place was uneatable, so we sent it back and ordered pasta instead.
examples.professional: The caterer's first tasting was so uneatable that our team rejected the contract for the conference.
examples.analytical: The argument may be logically consistent, but its conclusion is uneatable for anyone who values human dignity.

nuance.analogy: Uneatable is like a song you cannot finish listening to: the taste makes you stop.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus eatable, from eat, from Old English etan.
common_mistakes: Using uneatable for poisonous or non-food items; inedible is the better word for those.
Stressing the first syllable instead of EE.

senses.definition: The state of having no job; joblessness.
senses.example: Unemployment made Jack depressed.

senses.definition: The phenomenon of joblessness in an economy.
senses.example: Unemployment has been considered a cause of crime.

senses.definition: The level of joblessness in an economy, often measured as a percentage of the workforce.
senses.example: Unemployment was reported at 5.2% in May, up from 4.9% in April.

senses.definition: A type of joblessness due to a particular economic mechanism.
senses.example: All unemployments, seasonal, frictional, cyclical, classical, whatever, mean that you're out of work.

senses.definition: An instance or period of joblessness.
senses.example: Until then his life had consisted of low-paying jobs, numerous unemployments, and drug use.

core.definition: The condition of being without a paid job, or the percentage of people who are looking for work but cannot find it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PLOY, with a light secondary stress on un. The -ment ending is weak, so say 'munt,' not 'ment.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in economic discussion, but it can carry worry, hardship or sympathy when used about a person or community.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unemployment' in news and economic talk, often with numbers, such as 'the unemployment rate.' In personal talk, people usually say 'out of work' or 'laid off' rather than 'unemployment.' 'Unemployment' also refers to unemployment benefits, the government payments for people who lose jobs.

distinctions.note: Unemployed is an adjective or description of a person; unemployment is the noun for the condition or the statistic.
Joblessness is the more personal or sociological term; unemployment is the standard economic term.
Underemployment means working fewer hours or in jobs below one's skill level; unemployment means having no paid work at all.

examples.everyday: Unemployment is pretty high in our town right now, so jobs are hard to find.
examples.professional: Unemployment dropped to 3.9 percent last quarter, so the labor market got tighter for our hiring plans.
examples.analytical: Structural unemployment can persist even when aggregate demand is strong, because skills and locations do not match open jobs.

nuance.analogy: Unemployment is like an empty chair in a full room: it shows where the economy has no place for someone yet.
nuance.etymology: From unemploy (to deprive of employment) plus -ment, from un- (not) plus employ.
common_mistakes: Using 'unemployment' as an adjective; use 'unemployed' to describe a person.
Confusing 'unemployment' with 'underemployment,' which means working fewer hours or below one's skill level.

senses.definition: In an unexpected manner.

core.definition: In a way that was not expected or foreseen; suddenly and without warning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress stays on PECT. The -ly ends in a clear long 'lee', and the -ed is a short 'id'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; often introduces an event that is surprising, whether good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to open a sentence or describe an event, as in 'Unexpectedly, the store was closed.' It is common in news, storytelling and everyday talk. In speech it often comes mid-sentence, and in writing it often opens a sentence.

distinctions.note: Suddenly focuses on speed and abruptness; unexpectedly focuses on the lack of prediction.
Surprisingly suggests the result is notable or contrary to what you would think; unexpectedly stresses that no one saw it coming.

examples.everyday: Traffic was unexpectedly light, so we got to the airport early.
examples.professional: Unexpectedly, the server crashed during the deployment, so we rolled back the release.
examples.analytical: The variable unexpectedly dominated the regression, which suggests a confound we had not modeled.

nuance.analogy: Like a light that switches on by itself: the surprise comes from the lack of any warning.
nuance.etymology: un- + expectedly, from Latin exspectare 'to look out for'.
common_mistakes: Dropping the d and saying 'unexpectly' instead of 'unexpectedly'.
Using the adjective 'unexpected' where the adverb is needed, as in 'It happened unexpected'.

senses.definition: In a manner that is unfair.
senses.example: The carnival games were unfairly difficult, and hardly anybody won a prize.

core.definition: In a way that treats someone unjustly or not equally; in a manner that is not fair.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, FAIR, and the first syllable is weak, so it sounds like 'uhn', not 'UN'. The r in 'fair' is pronounced clearly in General American.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals that someone was treated badly or that a rule or result was unjust.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unfairly' constantly in everyday speech, especially with verbs like treat, accuse, criticize or judge. It is often used to protest, as in 'That's not fair' or 'You're being unfair to me.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, that's rough' or 'I know, it really isn't fair.'

distinctions.note: Unjustly stresses a violation of law, rights or moral principle and is more formal; unfairly is everyday and can refer to smaller matters like a game or a grade.
Wrongly focuses on a factual or moral mistake; unfairly focuses on unequal or biased treatment.

examples.everyday: My little brother got grounded for the whole weekend, and honestly that felt really unfairly harsh.
examples.professional: I think the reviewers scored our proposal unfairly because they misread the methodology section.
examples.analytical: A distributive rule that treats equally situated people unfairly violates the principle of equal consideration.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who calls fouls only on one team, an unfairly handled situation tilts the outcome.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus fairly, from Old English fæger, meaning beautiful or pleasing, later 'just'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'unfair' as an adverb instead of 'unfairly' (e.g., 'He was treated unfair').
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'UN' with full stress instead of a weak 'uhn'.

senses.definition: Joined into a single entity.
senses.example: The two companies merged into one united organization last spring after months of negotiation.

senses.definition: Involving the joint activity of multiple agents.
senses.example: The two parties stood united against the proposal.

core.definition: Joined together into one group, acting or thinking together toward the same goal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the final '-ed' is a short 'id' in this adjective. The 't' between vowels is often a quick flap, so it can sound close to 'yoo-NY-did'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests harmony, solidarity, and agreement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'united' in phrases like 'a united front', 'united effort', and in the proper name 'the United States'. The adjective describes a group that has come together, while 'unified' describes something made into one system. In casual speech, 'on the same page' may be a more natural alternative.

distinctions.note: Unified often describes a system or organization made into one structure, while united describes people or groups who act together with shared feeling or purpose.
Joint describes an action shared between two or more parties, while united describes a group that has become one in purpose or spirit.
Combined simply means added together, while united implies a stronger sense of shared commitment.

examples.everyday: Our family is pretty united when it comes to Thanksgiving, so nobody argues about the menu anymore.
examples.professional: The team came into the launch meeting united on the date, which made the review much smoother.
examples.analytical: A united community is not necessarily a uniform one, so the claim that a people is united depends on which shared commitments they actually hold.

nuance.analogy: Like several rivers merging into one stream that flows in a single direction.
nuance.etymology: From Latin unitus, the past participle of unire ('to unite').
common_mistakes: Writing 'united States' with a lowercase u in the proper name 'United States'.
